Friendly greetings!

I'm a longtime Sleeping Dogs fan and I like being immersed in this gameworld so much, I decided to mosey over into Triad Wars. I find raiding is a therapeutic exercise that feels hypnotic when I get into the rhythm of beating up thugs. Since raids are time trials, it pays (literally) to be swift and aim to complete 2 or even all 3 objectives on each go. In the process, I made it to Dragon Head, and I wanted to share these tips with you. Please do chime in with your own! In no particular order:

  • For my playstyle, I find that upgrading running speed and health regen (both of them) skills are extremely important. Every second counts, and that includes being able to dash from one racket to the next.

  • I really like using the meat cleaver with extra durability. Some of you are already familiar with cleaver-hopping — jumping from one opponent to the next and striking downward. With upgraded strength, you can take out a whole room pretty quickly.

  • The grenade launcher is very useful for clearing a tight space, just make sure you stand behind the door frame and don't be caught in the explosion. With a single hit, you can kill all enemy thugs.

  • It helps to reload a gun, especially a slow-reloading one like the shotgun, when you're running up stairs and between a racket's levels.

  • Decide on your goals before entering an enemy's turf — are you focused on leveling up, gaining face, or what? I'm primarily concerned with leveling and acquiring resources because face can more easily be lost.

  • It seems like raiding human opponents gets you a lot more face than the computer ones. Their turf is also interesting because I've come across various ones where one racket was quite well-developed while most others were lower-level. Those quirks can make them easier to conquer.

  • I generally prefer to rush in all the way to the furthest back rackets, prioritize which ones I want to hit (if I'm not using a time booster favor) based on what I need, then work my way back towards the entrance/exit. The reason is because this makes it easier to escape with less time, should you need to run.

  • If you're out of time and the cops rush in, if your gangster is strong enough, make the best of a bad situation and kill as many thugs as you can to level up before exiting. Cops will interfere and it may be a better idea to use guns, given their propensity to arrest you (causing you to lose everything), but thugs will also distract cops.

  • I like the peach wood sword's rapid striking and it feels very fluid to use, but it breaks all too easily. This would've been my favorite melee weapon were it not for that, so I stick with the cleaver.

  • Seems obvious, but learn to headshot with guns. Practice the vault shooting range at your turf. Makes for fewer wasted bullets and it's much quicker. In fact, when you slowly enter a room to scope out what weapons the thugs have, if you're quick with a gun, you can headshot several of them before they rush you. Even rushing makes for an opportunity because they're not hiding behind furniture and their face becomes a larger target while they get closer.

  • For those reasons, keep your distance with guns as well. It's a nuisance if you're in a room full of guys with guns and someone called for reinforcements earlier. One barefisted attacker can ruin your rhythm and expose you to further damage from guns, so you'll probably want to take a distraction like that out before proceeding.

  • Not a raid efficiency tip, but randomly (it seems) parked outside of some enemy turf will be a fast car you'll see after successfully completing a raid. This can make it very easy to enter a race mission after and win. I really like the Blast car, hence its hame.

  • In a space with not too many high objects to obscure thugs, a quick way to take out multiple thugs is to click middle mouse button to change to the focus mode, then quickly fire. Now, it's not anywhere near as accurate as headshots, but provided you've freshly reloaded and have lots of bullets, you can mow down a group pretty quickly.

  • Sometimes it can save time to kill all thugs in adjacent or nearby rackets outside, especially when your combat meter is active.

  • But remember, combat meter and special attacks do slow you down in a way, since the timer continues to count down, even while it shows those fancy animations. It's for that reason that especially on higher levels where your character has more innate power, that I eschew throwing thugs into environmental objects. Each one of those animations takes like 2-4 seconds. Much quicker to headshot or cleaver-chop 'em.

  • If you've decided to go after the rival enforcer, at least when you're starting out to intermediate, leave 2:00-3:00 left or so before storming the temple. You can get more aggressive once you're used to the patterns. Weapon availability and other variables can make a huge difference but just to allow room for error. Certain predictable props show up often, like the two gongs in the courtyard and the broken elevator and flat board you can throw people into right before heading up.

  • Weapon preparedness counts for a lot, I can't emphasize this enough: while your character is busy engaged in various animations, use the mouse to change camera perspective and observe what else is present. Was there a weapon recently dropped you should go for after killing the current thug? What way is it to the next level entrance? Planning ahead in the moment will help your moves be more liquid. Getting your timing thrown off while trying to clear a room of thugs really sucks! Combat can be pretty fun in the game but remember some actions are visibly delayed and don't happen all at once, like when you right-click to block a flashing red counterattack.

  • There are almost always three thugs present at the entrance of a rival turf. When driving I usually try to wipe them all out with my car, unless I want some combat practice. Plus, "In Pain Is Victory" health regen is great because if you forgot to heal at a food vendor, you can let those thugs sucker punch you a few times to gain more health than you lost.

  • You can drive a car into most turf, though it's unwieldy and rackets tend to have those yellow dividers that block cars from ramming into everyone.

  • Be very aware of where explodable gas tanks are! They can either help or hinder you. Sometimes, you'll come across several thugs positioned near one while you have a melee weapon out. Make sure you back away a safe distance (since those explosions can be insta-kill, especially on lower levels), quickly switch to a gun before they can run away and/or rush you, then blow 'em all up!

  • May be a bug, but some tables near entrances of gun-wielding thug levels seem to be un-vaultable over, but being higher may be an advantage to see others easier, if you're bold and can take the damage.

  • Though you may be in a hurry, certain pauses will help you out, like backing a way a bit before picking up a weapon by holding R, since if you're too near a thug, it can be confused or the thug can counter-attack and hurt you.

  • I suppose another useful thing to do whilst fighting is quickly scan to see if the racket has a next floor or if the door is blocked off/nonexistent. That can help you prepare. I find having sound on is very important because there are musical cues/riffs that let you know when an entire racket is cleared.

  • In most cases, it saves time to jump off the building and proceed to the next racket, instead of going back down all the stairs. I haven't found the right key combo to make sure you land on your feet instead of falling on your side and rolling (which costs time), maybe it's height-dependent but if anyone knows, chime in please.
Tips for faster, efficient, more awesome raiding!

I've only read parts of heidegger's work. Is there something of his you'd recommend? I can get a picture of his view on being using a rudimentary understanding of his "Hermeneutic Cycle", but it doesn't feel right, you know?

And with that, you have pretty much all that's really known about being. That's much of the point of "cogito ergo sum." Simply because one can reason regarding being, one can safely presume that being is reality. You can at least know that the mere fact that you can say "I genuinely am not sure" means that there's actually is an "I" that can observe and communicate that. The rest of the point of cogito ergo sum, or maybe more accurately the reason that it still resonates, is that that's all that one can really know. Everything beyond that is necessarily speculative and uncertain.

You can't even really know that the reality you perceive actually exists at all, since you don't directly experience it. Instead, your mind communicates an experience of it - your mind reports sight and touch and taste and smell - incidents and vistas and experiences and observations - but the "I" that analyzes it all and registers uncertainty does not directly experience any of that. So you're immediately and apparently irrevocably removed from the possibility of certain knowledge about any of it.

That said, it's practical to presume that that which you perceive exists. I personally like the Philip K Dick measure of that - "Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away." Again, you can't truly know that to be the case, but it's a safe bet.

And from that, one can at least speculate relatively reasonably, even about the nature of being.

To do that though, I find it helpful to break it down to much simpler little bits and pieces of the larger issue.

I read an argument recently that questions cogito ergo sum. What if I learn that I am schizophrenic, and slowly lose my ability to think/reason? What if ideas and concepts become strands that I pin to my coat to hopelessly stir and mix and spit back out again? Do I cease to be? Have I died? (do you stop being when you die?)

Interestingly enough I found this argument in David Duchovny's senior thesis: The Schizophrenic Critique of Pure Reason in Beckett's Early Novels

I don't see how any of that calls cogito ergo sum into question though.

The whole point really is simply that the mere fact that one can consider the concept "I" - entirely regardless of how one considers it or how accurate one's judgment of it might or might not be - demonstrates the existence of some manner of "I" that's doing that considering. Accuracy or the lack thereof regarding the specific nature of that "I" is irrelevant.

What you're working at here is a separate issue really - not simply whether or not there is an "I", but whether or not the "I" that one perceives is in fact the "I" that one believes it to be. And that immediately gets into a morass of subjectivism.

Personally, I would say that it's a pretty sure bet that there is no human being with a pure and complete and inerrant conception of self - that there is no human being whose sense of "I" is wholly accurate. But that's just my supposition.

As to whether or not the discovery that one's conception of "I" means that "I" have died, that would depend on the definitions of "I" and "died" one was using. By the most common definitions - no, that wouldn't be the case, in part because the existence of an "I" who was pondering whether or not "I" had ceased to exist would necessarily indicate that "I" in fact had not, but even more so because "died" indicates the termination of biological life - not simply a change in self-assessment.

In a less literal sense - with a bit of poetic license - sure. One could certainly say that "I" "died" when "I" discovered that "I" was someone other than who "I" had believed myself to be. That requires a pretty loose use of the term "died" though.
